entities.summary: François de Harlay de Champvallon was the fifth Archbishop of Paris, succeeding Jean-Henri-François de Bessencourt, who was appointed Archbishop by King Louis XIV in 1681. Champvallon's tenure was marked by his efforts to reform the Catholic Church in France, which included the establishment of a new cathedral and the creation of a seminary for the training of priests. He also played a key role in the development of the University of Paris, which became a center of learning and intellectual inquiry during the Enlightenment. Champvallon's legacy as a reformer and educator has endured, and he is remembered as one of the most important figures in the history of the Catholic Church in France. The French Revolution, which began in 1789, dealt a devastating blow to the Church, and Champvallon died in 1695, just before the Revolution's outbreak. Despite his untimely death, Champvallon's impact on the Church and French society continues to be felt. In 1683, Champvallon was elected Archbishop of Paris, a position he held until his death in 1695, and his efforts to reform the Church and promote education had a lasting impact on French Catholicism.
